passages.title: Learning the River's Language
passages.text:
The first time I paddled the Clearwater River with my aunt Rosa, I spent most of the trip staring at the bow of my kayak. Rosa, {{1|who has guided rafting trips for twenty years}} kept telling me to look up. "The river is talking," she said. "You just have to learn {{2|it's}} language."

Over the next summer, I began to understand what she meant. Between two submerged rocks {{3|lies}} the safest channel, marked by a smooth V pointing downstream. A V pointing upstream warns of a hidden boulder. Waves that curl back on themselves, called holes, can trap a {{4|boat, even}} a skilled paddler avoids them. Reading these signs {{5|quick}} became a habit; by August I was calling out hazards before Rosa did.

{{6|Kayaks can be made of plastic, fiberglass, or wood.}} Rosa taught me to check the gauge reports each morning, because a river that rises a foot overnight {{7|can, in a very short amount of time, transform}} a gentle stretch into a dangerous one. She kept a notebook of water levels going back a decade, and she could predict, almost to the hour, when the spring melt would peak.

On my last trip of the season, Rosa let me lead. I chose our line through every rapid, and twice I steered us around holes {{8|that were near the left bank.}} {{9|Watching me pick a line through the last rapid, a grin spread across Rosa's face.}} At the take-out, she handed me her notebook. "You'll need this more than I will," she said. {{10|I still have it.}} {{11|Its pages are filled with numbers, and in every one I can hear the river talking.}}

passages.title: The Last Sign Painter in Calder
passages.genre: profile (original; Calder and Marrow are invented)
passages.text:
In the river town of Calder, nearly every storefront sign was painted by hand, and most of them {{1|was}} painted by the same woman. For forty years, Edith Marrow climbed ladders with a {{2|brush a can of enamel, and a steady hand}}, lettering the names of bakeries, barbershops, and hardware stores {{3|onto there}} windows and walls.

Marrow learned the trade from her father, who {{4|had painted signs}} for the town since before she was born. {{5|He taught her to mix colors, to space letters by eye, and that a sign should be read from across the street.}} She practiced on scrap boards in the garage, painting the alphabet hundreds of times until her strokes were {{6|identical; even}} her father could not tell them from his own.

When vinyl lettering machines arrived in the 1990s, many of Marrow's customers switched. The machines were faster and {{7|cheaper, however,}} the stickers they produced {{8|got kind of messed up}} within a few years. One by one, the shop owners came back. "A machine can make a letter," one barber told a reporter, "but it can't make a sign."

Today Marrow is in her seventies and no longer climbs ladders. {{9|Still, she enjoys gardening and reading in her spare time.}} {{10|Her students, many of whom are young and in their twenties,}} say they come for the craft but stay for the patience it teaches.

passages.title: Mapping the Dark
passages.text:
When most people imagine cave exploration, they picture squeezing through tight passages in search {{1|for}} undiscovered chambers. The work that occupies most cavers, however, is slower and less glamorous: making maps. {{2|Without a map, a cave that has been explored is, for practical purposes, a cave that has been lost.}}

A survey team usually has three members. The first sets a station—a small numbered marker—at a point the others can see. {{3|The second, who holds a laser rangefinder, measures}} the distance to the station, while the third reads the compass bearing and the slope. {{4|Each of these numbers are recorded}} in a waterproof notebook, along with a sketch of the passage's walls.

[1] Back on the surface, the numbers become a map. [2] A single misread digit can send that path through solid rock. [3] Software converts each set of measurements into a line segment, and the segments, joined end to end, trace the cave's path. [4] For this reason, many teams measure every leg twice, once in each direction.

The work is slow. A team might survey only a few hundred meters in a long day, {{5|and the rangefinders run on rechargeable batteries}}. {{6|Yet}} cavers keep at it, {{7|year after year, decade after decade, for many years}}, because a good map is the one discovery that lasts: {{8|its useful}} to every caver, scientist, and rescue team that enters the cave afterward. {{9|Whom}} else would bother to do it?

passages.text:
The letters arrived in a shoebox the summer after my grandmother died: forty-three of them, written in Portuguese to her sister in the Azores and returned to our family after the {{1|sisters'}} deaths. I had studied Portuguese for two years in high school, and I assumed that would be enough. It was not.

My grandmother wrote the way she talked, in long sentences full of village nicknames and expressions I could not find in any dictionary. {{2|For example,}} she called the town's priest "the Rooster," and she described a hard winter as "a winter with teeth." Some pages took me an entire evening. On one, she had copied a few lines by the Portuguese {{3|poet, Fernando Pessoa,}} into the margin, and next to them she had written a single word {{4|that, I eventually translated as}} "exactly."

I began keeping a notebook of the phrases I could not translate, and by the end of the summer it held more than two hundred entries. At first, the notebook felt like a list of failures. Gradually it became something else: a record of {{5|the way, my grandmother saw}} the world, one stubborn phrase at a time. {{6|The notebook had cost three dollars at a drugstore.}}

I still cannot read Portuguese {{7|fluently. I can}}, however, recognize my grandmother's voice in it, {{8|which took me most of a long summer}}. Last month I {{9|lended}} the notebook to my cousin, who is starting on the letters herself.

questions.stem: Suppose the writer's goal had been to show how translating the letters changed the narrator's understanding of the grandmother. Would this essay accomplish that goal?

choices.A: Yes, because the work of translating leads the narrator to recognize the grandmother's voice and outlook.
choices.B: Yes, because it explains in detail the grammar rules the narrator mastered while translating.
choices.C: No, because it focuses mainly on the history of the Azores rather than on the grandmother.
choices.D: No, because the narrator never finishes translating the letters and remains unable to read them.

questions.explanation: The notebook turns from a list of failures into a record of how the grandmother saw the world, and the narrator learns to recognize her voice: a changed understanding.
